title: Sunderland teen Beau-Jack Mensforth blackmailed girls to self-harm
description: This aticle contains distressing detailsA "cowardly monster" who blackmailed girls across the world into self-harming for the entertainment of others
body: This aticle contains distressing detailsA "cowardly monster" who blackmailed girls across the world into self-harming for the entertainment of others has been detained for 14 and a half years.Beau-Jack Mensforth was 17 when he began forcing vulnerable girls to send sexual images, hurt animals and carve his assumed name into their bodies, Newcastle Crown Court heard.One of the girls' mothers said he used the internet to breach the safety of his victims' homes and minds, causing lifelong devastation.Mensforth, 20 and from Sunderland, admitted 17 offences. They included crimes against nine victims, the youngest of whom was aged 12, and having indecent images of children as young as five. Mensforth was in online groups who made content for their "com", short for community, by victimising "vulnerable young girls", prosecutor Charlotte Hole said.They often targeted girls in self-harm support groups and used apps including Telegram and Discord to befriend them.Abusers convinced the girls they were in romantic relationships and coaxed them into sending indecent images of themselves, then threatened to publish the pictures unless they committed more "extreme" acts, the court heard.If you are affected by any issues raised, help can be found through BBC Action LineThe girls would be forced to carve the names of their abusers into their flesh and write messages and logos in blood promoting the "com" groups.They were also ordered to "sacrifice" animals under the threat their personal information would be released online or false reports would be made to trigger armed police raids of their homes.Under the username Yuri, Mensforth targeted girls in the UK, USA and Australia, making them write "I worship Yuri" in blood among a litany of other abuses.When one of his victims asked him why he was doing it, Mensforth replied "for content", the court heard, with the abuser seeking to rise to the top of the group's hierarchy.A victim from the USA said she was 16 when she was "lured" into Mensforth's "online child predator group".Having been forced to harm herself, the pictures of her "mutilated" body then got thousands of views online, she said.She said she begged her abusers to take the images down but they refused, adding: "The more I cried about it the more amusement it seemed to bring them."Her mother said she had no idea there were "cowardly monsters" like Mensforth "hiding behind a screen tormenting our baby girl".A UK-based victim, who was 13 when Mensforth began abusing her, reported him to police."Instead of looking back at my early teen years and being filled with joy, I'm reminded of the fear and violation I felt," she said.Her body was "covered" with scars inflicted at Mensforth's behest, she said, describing him as a "psychopath" who "feeds off the pain" of others. Other victims said they had ongoing mental health issues and their trauma was worse because the images were still online.Mensforth admitted blackmail, sexual communications with children, making and distributing indecent images of children and participating in an organised crime group between 2023 and 2024.Judge Edward Bindloss said Mensforth was a "calculating predator" who groomed, manipulated and blackmailed girls for those who shared his "taste for sexual violence and enjoyed watching females self-harm".Mensforth "rose to play a leading role" in the harm group and "thrived" on his status, the judge said.Bindloss said Mensforth, who told probation workers he hoped to push a girl into killing herself, would have to serve six years on extended licence.Follow BBC Sunderland on X, external, Facebook, external, Nextdoor and Instagram, external.

title: 'Poison seller' Kenneth Law apologises in court to the families of his victims
description: The Canadian man who sold toxic chemicals through online suicide forums in 40 countries apologised in court to the families of the victims, saying he
body: The Canadian man who sold toxic chemicals through online suicide forums in 40 countries apologised in court to the families of the victims, saying he deeply regrets his actions and will never repeat them.Kenneth Law made the remarks on Friday during a sentencing hearing where prosecutors asked a judge to give him a 25-year prison term. The 61-year-old pleaded guilty in May to 14 counts of aiding the suicide deaths of 14 people in Ontario, Canada, though he has admitted to causing the deaths of dozens of victims in England and Wales.He will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths under a plea deal which saw Canadian authorities withdraw more serious charges of murder. During Friday's sentencing hearing in an Ontario court, prosecutors stressed that many of his victims were young and struggling with mental distress.If Law receives the prosecution's recommended sentence, he would serve just under 20 years in prison, after accounting for credit for time served since his May 2023 arrest.As she sought to make her case in court on Friday, Crown Attorney Kathleen Doherty described Law as a predator taking advantage of "vulnerable people". "What they needed was help. But what they found was Mr Law and his products for death," Doherty said.She also said Law's motives were financial. "If people could pay, he sold it to them. There's no discussion or inquiries or anything going on whereby Mr Law would have any ability to appreciate the circumstances of the individual he was dealing with," she said.Law's defence lawyer, Matthew Gourlay, countered those claims, arguing that his client was not responsible for any of their battles with mental illness.. "Each of these incidents is its own unique tragedy," Gourlay said. "Mr Law may be a common denominator between them, but Mr Law was not the cause of the struggles and hardships that caused all these victims to seek out his products in the first place." He said Law held a "misguided belief" he was helping his victimsLaw's defence attorney has asked the court to give him a 12-year sentence. At the end of the hearing, Law told the court that he had deep regret for aiding in the suicide deaths of his victims. "To the families of the victims, words can never replace the loss of your loved ones. I convey my deepest condolences. I remain remorseful. I'm sorry."The sentencing hearing followed an emotional few days of testimony in September, when grieving family members and friends told the court of the pain Law had caused. Those impact statements will be taken into account at sentencing, which is due at a later date.Authorities said the former chef sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients - who he met in online suicide forums - in 40 countries, roughly a quarter of which were sent to the UK.If you or anyone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this article, details of organisations offering information are available at BBC Action Line

title: Turkish officials 'destroyed' pro-opposition TV channel, owner tells BBC
description: Turkish authorities have "destroyed" one of the country's most-watched news channels, its London-based owner has told the BBC.Speaking to the BBC's Ne
body: Turkish authorities have "destroyed" one of the country's most-watched news channels, its London-based owner has told the BBC.Speaking to the BBC's Newshour, Cafer Mahiroğlu said that nine people connected to Halk TV were arrested this week on charges including money laundering, bribery and spreading misleading information.Mahiroğlu said that several of his family members were among those arrested when the pro-opposition channel was taken into government control last month, adding that the allegations against him and Halk TV are "completely wrong".The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor' Office said that two former news anchors of the channel were among the most recent group of people detained.In a statement, prosecutors accused the anchors of producing "false reports" in exchange for money.Authorities have also issued an arrest warrant for the channel's news coordinator Kürşad Oğuz who is "abroad", the statement said, without specifying where.Mahiroğlu told the BBC that he could be sent to prison if he tried to return to Turkey."[The government] wants to be in control of the whole media... I'm more worried about my country and my democracy than my channel," he said.The headquarters of Halk TV was raided by Turkish authorities last month, halting the channel's live broadcasts, the latest in a series of crackdowns on news sources deemed to be critical of Turkish President Tayyip Erdoğan and his administration. The government subsequently appointed a new administrator to run the channel.Erdoğan's government controls much of the country's media, which ranks among the worst globally for press freedom, external, though the government insists that it does not detain media workers for carrying out journalistic activities.However, the president has scaled up a crackdown on dissent since his narrow victory in the 2023 presidential election.  Earlier this month, authorities took control of pro-opposition network Sozcu TV.Erdoğan's main challenger, mayor of Istanbul Ekrem Imamoğlu, has been jailed on corruption charges and for violating election laws, which he and his party have fiercely denied. Hundreds of Imamoğlu's supporters have faced similar accusations, while the government has also imprisoned other campaigners, lawyers and comedians.

schema.headline: Turkish officials 'destroyed' pro-opposition TV channel, owner tells BBC

title: 'We couldn't give up that easily': Marching bands scramble to cover costs after Thanksgiving parade rearranged
description: Figure caption, How New York reacted to postponement of Macy's paradeByJames FitzGeraldFreya Scott-Turner and Brandon DrenonSince New York City offici
body: Figure caption, How New York reacted to postponement of Macy's paradeByJames FitzGeraldFreya Scott-Turner and Brandon DrenonSince New York City officials postponed the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, a precaution ahead of a storm that brought heavy rain, wind and flooding, hundreds of touring performers who traveled from across the US to perform were thrust into chaos."It was jarring," said Ryan Demkovich, director of a Texas high school marching band. After learning the news, he had to scramble to make new arrangements for over 500 people. Demkovich and his Pearland High School band made the quick decision to launch a fundraiser, reaching $350,000 (£267,000) in just a few hours. Still, some performers reportedly had to skip the parade, a televised, traditional Thanksgiving event - now rescheduled for Saturday.On Wednesday afternoon, a day before the event, organisers announced the postponement, in part due to concerns around the parade's giant balloons in strong winds.The balloons, inflated on Wednesday, were then temporarily deflated - along with  the spirits of those who journeyed to the city to watch the action.The move represented the first time the event had been postponed in its 100-year history, although it was suspended altogether during World War II.Each year, a number of marching bands travel from across the country, from high schools and colleges, to perform at the event. This is considered a huge opportunity, as the parade is watched by millions in person and on TV.Demkovich described an emotional and exhausting experience, first learning that the parade would be postponed while watching a Broadway performance of Wicked with his band. "My initial thought was like, 'Oh, crap. We're not going to be able to go'," he said. "Where are we going to be able to get all the money for this?" The delay meant unexpected expenses of additional nights in a hotel - and meals - for hundreds of people in the middle of New York City during the holidays. There were no vacancies to extend their stay at the New York Marriott Marquis in Times Square, so they booked the nearest hotel with availability - across the Hudson River - in New Jersey.Demkovich said the Pride of Pearland Marching Band posted a fundraiser online and within hours met its fundraising goal."The word just spread like wildfire, truly like wildfire," Demkovich said, adding that donations came from over 2,000 people and local businesses. He called the outpouring of support "very, very overwhelming to think about and comprehend"."We have a lot to be thankful for this Thanksgiving."Some groups were not able to maneuver as easily. The University of Alabama's Million Dollar Band is one of those missing out, due to a schedule conflict on Saturday.“‘This can’t be happening’,” Rina Browder, mother of a snare drummer in the band, told local news, describing the band’s reactions."They were devastated. They've worked so hard for this. So many practices."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The Pride of Pearland Marching Band from Texas - pictured rehearsing earlier this week - said it raised hundreds of thousands of dollarsMeanwhile, a group from Hawaii, the Nā Koa Aliʻi Hawaiʻi All-State Marching Band, said it too would still be able to participate in the parade, also because of emergency fundraising by families, friends and other supporters donating more than $500,000.Speaking to the BBC on Thursday, the group's director Rickey H Badua described the time pressures. "We are racing to get this done," he explained. The band is made up of hundreds of musicians from dozens of schools across the state. It travelled almost 5,000 miles (8,000km) to get to New York."Getting the news that we got the parade postponed was not easy, and emotional for our students," Badua said.But the musicians sprang into action quickly, he said. "We come from a very far place," Badua said, adding that "to get so close to the finish line and not show up for it, we couldn't give up that easily".The response from friends and family had been "incredible", he said.Figure caption, New York City mayor on postponing 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day ParadeBadua was hopeful his group would have the same experience he had when he first performed at the parade in 2003, as student drum major. "The energy is palpable, people are just excited to see a band that is great."Another musical act, from Illinois, told the BBC on Thursday it needed to raise  $175,000 to cover another night in a hotel, additional food, and bus costs back to the city of Champaign."Things are going well due to the very generous support of so many amazing human beings," said Professor Barry Houser, director of the University of Illinois Marching Illini.By Friday, 3,500 donors had stepped up to help the 410 students and their travel party. "This is truly phenomenal," said Houser.While awaiting the parade, musicians and punters alike have sheltered from the heavy wind and rain brought by the storm to eastern areas of the US.Hundreds of thousands of homes were without power in the storm's aftermath Friday, and coastal areas had flooded. The National Weather Service (NWS) expects conditions to improve gradually on Friday.Additional reporting by Jessica MurphyFigure caption, Watch: Roofs torn off and streets under water as severe weather hits the US

schema.headline: 'We couldn't give up that easily': Marching bands scramble to cover costs after Thanksgiving parade rearranged

title: Dec Donnelly says I'm a Celebrity tension 'became much bigger deal than it should have'
description: Frostrup apologised during an amicable conversation on Tuesday, and Odudu accepted, explaining it was "triggering" because "it's a strong word to use
body: Frostrup apologised during an amicable conversation on Tuesday, and Odudu accepted, explaining it was "triggering" because "it's a strong word to use in casual scenarios, particularly towards black women". On their podcast, Hanging Out with Ant and Dec, Donnelly said tensions in camp started "surprisingly early". "From day one cooking was tense and then it obviously came to a head with AJ and Mariella, and it spilled over to breakfast the next morning," he said.McPartlin added: "You have 12 hungry mouths to feed and you and your sous chef, the other chef, are cooking and everyone is stood around looking at them. The pressure is quite a lot."Donnelly continued: "When you are there, and so much of your life revolves around that mealtime, it's the only meal of the day you really get that isn't rice and beans."There is a lot of pressure and obviously Mariella was feeling that pressure."AJ wanted to come in and help and it all came to a head, and maybe because there was so much pressure and because it was so important, Mariella maybe didn't handle it very well around the campfire when she was cooking, and it spilled over into the next day - and it became a much bigger deal than it should have done."He said the "most important thing" was that "the two ladies were able to sit down and drew a line under it, they were adult enough to sit there, talk it through, and move on together. If more people did that the world would be a much better place".McPartlin agreed, saying: "If some of our leaders did that, the world would be a better place."On Wednesday, an Ofcom spokesperson told BBC News: "We are assessing the complaints against our rules, but are yet to decide whether or not to investigate."On Thursday night, Frostrup completed her fourth bushtucker trial, which is voted for by the public. Many viewers defended Odudu after the encounter.They included broadcaster and comic Judi Love who said she felt "triggered by Frostrup's comment, while Britain's Got Talent judge Alesha Dixon and Strictly Come Dancing judge Motsi Mabuse also gave their support to Odudu.BBC Radio 1 DJ Clara Amfo said: "Calling a black woman 'aggressive' when she is being anything else but is a classic microaggression."Speaking on spin-off show I'm A Celebrity... Unpacked on Sunday, former campmate Jordan Banjo said Frostrup had handled the situation "poorly", but urged people to "give a bit of grace to Mariella, and everyone in the camp" because "you can't judge an abnormal situation by normal standards".It is "a really weird situation that every single person's in, and I'm not sure if people go at stuff with the clearest head", he said, explaining: "You get these weird breakdowns, and I think that's what we're seeing."

schema.headline: Dec Donnelly says I'm a Celebrity tension 'became much bigger deal than it should have'

title: Zelensky tells BBC US too focused on Middle East and not pushing Russia hard enough
description: Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, criticising Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin "my friend" and saying delays in deliv
body: Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, criticising Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin "my friend" and saying delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles were costing Ukrainian lives.In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president complained the US was not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks, and called it "strange" that Trump posted a photo of himself embracing Putin."Of course it's up to the president of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English."He's an aggressor, and a killer... He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, adding it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during World War Two.Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the US.Trump's two envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, said on Wednesday that Putin had shown "restraint" by not using nuclear weapons in Ukraine. He also described Putin as a "grand master of politics".The latest round of peace talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this month made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.He said talks were expected to resume in December.On Thursday, Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions – on everything.And Zelensky revealed that it was not clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced.The Kremlin appears to be resisting.Ukraine urgently needs the talks to move forward and bring five exhausting years of Russia's full-scale invasion to an end.Russian strikes across the country have been growing more frequent and more deadly: the number of civilians being killed is at an all-time high.So Zelensky called for "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve results and urged the US to live up to its reputation as a strong country with "power and respect"."When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he said.The US argues that it is neutral: in the complex search for a peace deal between the two sides that can hold.Questioned again on Thursday about calling Putin a friend, Trump told reporters: "We want to stop killing. I could say he's not a friend... I want to make a deal."He added: "I could walk in and say, I don't like you, and then we have the same problem that we have with Zelensky and Putin."You know... the biggest problem to that settlement is the fact that you have two leaders that really hate each other."In the meantime, Kyiv is struggling to defend its skies.The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.But there is a "very, very big" deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles and he said the Americans were delaying deliveries of its Patriot systems."It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them more… It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky said."The deficit of these missiles - that is people's lives."He also confirmed that the US satellite communications system, Starlink – and its military version, Starshield – were still being restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine.Ukrainian drone units have described their problems to the BBC, as their interceptor drones can no longer catch up with Russian Shaheds. It means those weapons then fly deeper into Ukraine, unhindered.So whose decision was that?"Technically SpaceX, politically - I don't know, I really don't know," Zelensky replied. "It's like... ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it's the other."Ukraine's own long-range strikes against Russian targets have increased in recent weeks, including oil refineries and ships carrying weapons or fuel.On Thursday, Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said an attack that sank a Russian warship docked in eastern Libya this week risked spreading war to the Mediterranean, which was unacceptable.Zelensky defended the move, calling the warship Merkury an "absolutely fair goal".He accepted that such strikes were "very dangerous" but said Ukraine's forces "never attack" without co-ordinating with its partners.He declined to be more specific.But he acknowledged that Ukraine was bracing for a difficult and dangerous winter.Recent attacks on Kyiv have targeted bridges over the vast river Dnipro, apparently trying to cut the city in two.Some residents have already left town for the winter and businesses closed, as power cuts and strikes on logistics networks have pushed operating costs unmanageably high.They have also plunged much of the city into darkness."[Russia] wants us to run away, of course," Zelensky said."People can go, but we will try to defend our capital in any way. We need our capital. Without a capital, you don't have a country."

schema.headline: Zelensky tells BBC US too focused on Middle East and not pushing Russia hard enough

title: 'We have no interest in hearing from Huw Edwards', Downing Street says
description: The prime minister's spokesperson has said broadcasters must "act responsibly" and that "we have no interest in hearing" what Huw Edwards has to say,
body: The prime minister's spokesperson has said broadcasters must "act responsibly" and that "we have no interest in hearing" what Huw Edwards has to say, following a backlash against new interviews with the disgraced former BBC News presenter.Edwards, who was convicted in 2024 for making indecent images of children, has been interviewed for a Channel 4 documentary plus a podcast by the Observer and Tortoise Media."Our thoughts first and foremost will be with the victims of child sexual abuse and exploitation. We have no interest in hearing what he has to say," a Downing Street spokesperson said."There are extremely serious crimes and anyone convicted of them must face the consequences of their actions."The No 10 spokesperson added that broadcasters "are expected to act responsibly and have appropriate regards to their audiences when making decisions".Pressed on whether the prime minister believed Channel 4 had not acted responsibly, they said: "Channel 4 is editorially independent and decisions about individual programmes and contributors are a matter for them."During the court case, Edwards admitted three counts of making indecent images of children. That involved having 41 images and videos, which were sent to him on WhatsApp – including some showing a victim aged between seven and nine.Earlier, Environment Minister Emma Hardy said the plan by Channel 4 made her feel "sick", telling LBC, external it was giving a platform to "someone who is on the Sex Offenders Register"."That platform doesn't exist for his child victims, does it?... It's not something I could support, and it's definitely not something I'd be watching."Channel 4 has defended the programme, telling the BBC a "highly experienced director", Patrick Forbes, held Edwards to account with "no questions off limits, revealing his account of what led to his offending and very public downfall".Conservative MP Dame Caroline Dinenage, chair of the House of Commons culture and media select committee, said the media outlets should "not just act as a platform" for Edwards to have a voice.Any programme featuring him "needs to properly challenge his past actions" she said, along with raising "still unanswered questions" about whether Edwards will return more than £200,000 he was paid by the BBC, after he was first arrested.The documentary and podcast will both be released on Tuesday, with some material expected to be published by the Observer on Sunday.The interviews have also been criticised by three people who previously spoke to BBC News about allegations of Edwards' inappropriate behaviour.One, who accused him in 2023 of sending them threatening messages, said it was "incredibly bizarre that anyone, big names like Channel Four, are platforming him when he's a convicted sex offender".The person, who is anonymous and not connected to the criminal case, told BBC News on Thursday Edwards was "clearly trying to do a bit of damage repair" and they were "annoyed that he's being able to air these opinions".Another person, who said Edwards sent them suggestive and "pushy" messages when they were working at the BBC, and was also not involved in the court case, said: "I'm pretty disgusted they are giving him the air time."Additionally, a former junior BBC employee, who previously told BBC Newsnight's Victoria Derbyshire they had received inappropriate messages from Edwards, said "it seems a strange and irresponsible decision to give a platform to tell his story after the crimes he has been found guilty of."I hope that consideration has been given to his victims."Duncan Craig, head of We Are Survivors, which supports male survivors of sexual abuse and rape, said it felt like the media companies were "not thinking about the victims in this particular case".And it is the wrong time to release these programmes, coming during "a reckoning moment" for abuse in the media, he added."[It is] in fact giving somebody a platform that, in some way, shape or form, gives them the ability to nail themselves to the cross. That is not OK."He added he does "fundamentally believe in rehabilitation" but that "this doesn't feel like it."In a promotional clip released by the Observer, interviewer Ceri Thomas is seen saying he was "just deeply curious about how it was that a man of such prominence had got himself into this unbelievable, terrible fix".Craig criticised that choice of words. "An 'unbelievable terrible fix' isn't somebody sat actively downloading 41 images of child sexual abuse, of which a number of them were at grade A level of of boys aged seven to nine being sexually abused," he said.BBC broadcaster Nicky Campbell added, external his voice, saying: "I'm rather more concerned for the children in the photographs. What of their lives?"The Observer, which is owned by Tortoise Media, has been asked for a response to the criticism.Meanwhile, journalist Sangita Myska posted, external: "The rehabilitation [of] Huw Edwards' reputation via a 'personal journey' documentary is contemptible. He's a sex offender. What the hell is Channel 4 thinking?"Fellow broadcaster Richard Bacon responded, external: "Why is that rehabilitation? It's a documentary. There are lots of them about lots of different people. About lots of different types of people."

schema.headline: 'We have no interest in hearing from Huw Edwards', Downing Street says

title: Satellite imagery shows how fast Lagos and Alexandria are sinking
description: New satellite data shows how fast some African cities are sinkingImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Four million people in Lagos, Nigeria may be
body: New satellite data shows how fast some African cities are sinkingImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Four million people in Lagos, Nigeria may be exposed to extreme sea levels by the end of the century, a new study saysByAlex BrianClimate and Science reporterSome of Africa's largest cities are sinking faster than previously thought, new research shows.Scientists used radar imagery from the European Space Agency's Sentinel-1 satellites to map how much the land beneath 20 African coastal cities had moved.The study found that some cities - including Lagos in Nigeria and Alexandria in Egypt - were sinking much faster than previously estimated in 2021 by the UN's climate body, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).While some causes of this sinking, or subsidence, are natural, many are the result of human activities, such as the extraction of groundwater from underneath the Earth's surface.Lead author Oluwaseyi Dasho said the effects of subsidence "are often invisible in everyday life, but over decades they can substantially increase flood exposure".This is because when the ground sinks it becomes lower relative to the ocean and adds to the risk of the sea level rises caused by climate change.Seven million people, one billion buildings and $180bn (£137bn) of assets could be at flood risk by 2050, the paper estimated.Satellites give a clearer pictureIn the past, a lack of monitoring stations has prevented scientists from obtaining up-to-date localised information on subsidence in Africa, Dasho said.But by using satellite data, the researchers from Virginia Tech were able to detect land movements as small as 1mm per year.Senior author Manoochehr Shirzaei said Sentinel-1 satellites flew over the same region of the Earth every six to 12 days."[The satellite] transmits the radar signal, which hits the ground and bounces back to the satellite," the geosciences professor explained. This process is then repeated on "many revisits".The time between sending the signal and receiving it back is recorded, with changes in this value over time revealing how much the land has moved.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, More of Alexandria could be exposed to flooding than previously thought, the research saysThe ground under Alexandria and Lagos was found to have sunk an average of 6mm and 5mm per year respectively.If this rate continued, sea levels around Alexandria would rise 36% more by 2050 than the IPCC predicted, external, under the middle estimates for how much planet-warming emissions will increase.Luanda in Angola has also sunk significantly, but other cities such as Durban in South Africa have remained stable or even risen slightly.Shirzaei said showing where the IPCC had underestimated risks - but also where the threat had been overestimated - could help planners allocate resources more effectively.Sinking caused by local activitiesThe man-made drivers of subsidence are usually "extremely local, [which] means that we can combat them by creating local policies", Shirzaei explained.One major cause is the increased water consumption of rapidly growing cities. Too much water being extracted from the ground can lead to the soil becoming compacted and the surface sinking.The Aswan Dam on the Nile may also be trapping sediment upstream and preventing the replacement of sinking land in Alexandria, the study suggests.In Lagos, the reclaiming of land from the ocean to create artificial islands and the construction of buildings on loose ground are other possible causes of subsidence.Why are some cities sinking?Hear from those trying to solve the problemMethods of preventing cities from sinking include supplying other water sources and growing less water-intensive crops."Whatever we cannot mitigate, we try to adapt to it," Shirzaei added. This could mean building flood defences or moving key infrastructure to a higher level.The professor said developing countries had been "left out" of much of the planning for sea-level rises due to a lack of monitoring.The techniques developed in this study could potentially be used to address the knowledge gap in other regions, such as the Pacific islands, Shirzaei suggested.Oluwaseyi Dasho said he hoped the paper, in Science Advances,, external could help African governments "prepare adequately for future challenges and more importantly for the future generations".

schema.headline: Satellite imagery shows how fast Lagos and Alexandria are sinking

title: Body found in woodland near Springholm confirmed as Kelsey Hunter
description: Image source, Kelsey Hunter/ FacebookImage caption, Police have confirmed that a body found in woodland near Springholm has been identified as Kelsey
body: Image source, Kelsey Hunter/ FacebookImage caption, Police have confirmed that a body found in woodland near Springholm has been identified as Kelsey HunterPolice have confirmed that a body found in woodland in southern Scotland has been identified as missing 20-year-old Kelsey Hunter.She had last been seen in Castle Douglas at 17:00 on Saturday and a major search was carried out around the nearby village of Springholm where she lived.On Tuesday, Daniel McKnight, 21, appeared on petition at Dumfries Sheriff Court charged with murder and two other charges, including defeating the ends of justice. Kelsey's body was found at about 19:15 on Wednesday.McKnight made no plea and was remanded in custody.The search operation around the Dumfries and Galloway village concluded when the body was found but police said extensive inquiries remained ongoing with a number of resources being used - including forensic specialists.Det Ch Insp Stephen McGrath said: "Our thoughts remain with Kelsey's family at this incredibly difficult time, and we are continuing to provide them with support."They have asked that their privacy is respected."Extensive work remains ongoing and a team of officers are continuing to carry out inquiries."Image source, Press AssociationImage caption, Police said forensic specialists were still involved in their inquiriesHe thanked everyone who had come forward with information so far and said officers would remain in the area while the investigation continued.Door-to-door and CCTV inquiries are still being carried out.Local area commander Emma Dodds said: "We understand how upsetting this has been for the local community, but we continue to have a significant amount of resources dedicated to this investigation.He asked anyone with any concerns, or information to contact police, external.Image caption, Support has been offered at the primary school near where a cordon has been in placeA large police presence has been in the village - which sits next to the A75 that runs from Gretna to Stranraer - since Sunday evening.Dogs, a helicopter and specialist officers were involved in the search while officers made door-to-door inquiries.Dumfries and Galloway Council has been offering support to the village primary which is close to where a police cordon was in place.It said a message had been sent to the community to reassure them that the school continued to be a "safe and nurturing space".The local authority's principal education psychologist has also been working with the primary and Castle Douglas High School to "provide support to learners and staff".

schema.headline: Body found in woodland near Springholm confirmed as Kelsey Hunter

title: Spanish PM and rivals rally supporters in final pitch for votes
description: If he gets to form a government this time, it will be with the support of anti-immigration party Vox, led by Santiago Abascal, whose final rally took
body: If he gets to form a government this time, it will be with the support of anti-immigration party Vox, led by Santiago Abascal, whose final rally took place in front of thousands of people in a bull-ring in Valencia on Spain's east coast.The venue was filled with Spanish flags and green Vox banners, and one of the biggest cheers of the night came when the secretary general of the party called for "less burka and less halal".Ignacio Garriga said he was not acting out of hatred but love for the homeland.A small section of the crowd could be heard chanting "Viva Franco" in reference to the dictator, whose death in 1975 heralded the start of Spain's transition to democracy.A number of first-time voters at the rally said they were supporting Vox because of its policies on immigration.Lledó, 18, said what had happened in Ceuta in the summer, when more than 70,000 migrants crossed into the Spanish territory from Morocco, showed Sánchez was not able to control the country's border.She had come to the bullring with her mum and aunt, Carli Chilet, who argued that Vox "are the best for women's rights".Vox is hoping to almost double its seats from the 33 it won three years ago. It backs policies such as "national priority" - putting Spanish citizens first for welfare - and "remigration" for foreigners not considered to be contributing to the economy.While the conservatives tried to turn the spotlight on the series of scandals that have overshadowed the Socialists' term in office, Sánchez and his left-wing ally Ada Colau, who heads Frente Amplio (The Broad Front), focused on women's rights.The two leaders seized on a moment in the debate when the PP leader accused Colau and the rest of the left of staying quiet during a flood disaster in Valencia, briefly moving his finger to his lips. The word he used "calladita" is a diminutive and can also be used to tell a woman to "keep quiet" in a condescending manner.Sánchez reacted immediately and called on him to show "a little respect", accusing him of sexism. Feijóo sought to clarify what he meant on Friday, and accused Ada Colau of remaining silent during "these years of corruption". His decision to wind up his campaign in Seville was significant, because the wider southern region of Andalusia has 61 seats in Spain's 350-seat parliament, more than any other.Andalusia is also important because it is run by a coalition made up of the PP and Abascal's Vox, as are three other regions, Extremadura, Aragón, and Castilla y León.Feijóo has insisted he wants to govern with a majority, backed up by "parliamentary support agreements" with Vox and says he has never spoken to Abascal about giving Vox ministerial power."Governing is about managing, and I have spent my whole life preparing for this moment," he said in Seville.One of his new supporters at the rally was a retired woman called Isabel who told Spanish public broadvaster RTVE that she was attending a PP rally for the first time. The formerly loyal Socialist voter said she was "disillusioned" with a party led by  Sánchez. Another voter at the rally said Spain needed "a good manager".Sánchez took to the stage in Madrid with his wife Begoña Gómez, and donned a red T-shirt that read "power of the people". He then went on to praise Colau and her left-wing coalition's campaign. "These elections are about moving Spain forward, not taking it backwards," he said.Socialist supporter Leon Felipe, 25, told Reuters news agency: "Well, I think what's at stake in these elections is a big deal, is not a change of government... but rather a return to the past - a return to Franco's dictatorship. "So, I believe that young must mobilise."As he was speaking, Colau told a large audience in the south of Madrid that not only would they "not remain silent, we will win", vowing to form another "progressive government".

schema.headline: Spanish PM and rivals rally supporters in final pitch for votes

title: Newspaper headlines: 'This is for the kiddies' and 'Benefits and pensions chaos'
description: People claiming benefits and pensions have faced "chaos", says the Guardian, external, after the cyber incident which took some government services of
body: People claiming benefits and pensions have faced "chaos", says the Guardian, external, after the cyber incident which took some government services offline. The paper says it has fuelled concerns about the government's ability to "defend itself against malicious attacks", with experts telling the Daily Mail, external it could have been the work of a hostile state. One cyber-security boss in the FT Weekend, external says it raises questions about "how resilient the systems underpinning everyday life really are".The Times, external leads with the news that all schools in England will be required to give pupils time to read for pleasure. Education secretary Lucy Powell says "we cannot afford to stand idly by" while literacy and reading levels fall. The report also says that the education "overhaul" will include a slimming down of GCSEs, which could lead to some exams being shorter.Figures published in the Daily Telegraph, external show that nearly half a million rental properties were taken off online portals in just 10 months, after the government launched what the paper terms a "crackdown on landlords". The Ministry of Housing calls the data, from the landlord body, Propertymark, misleading."Kate reveals darkest times of cancer fight" is the headline in the Daily Mail, external which reports on the new documentary featuring the Princess of Wales. According to the Daily Express, external, one emotional scene shows Catherine wiping away tears as she watches video messages from her children, who she says gave her a reason to get out of hospital. The Daily Mirror's, external headline is: "This is for the kiddies".And the Sun, external says that James Bond bosses are considering the comedian David Mitchell for the role of the gadget master, Q. An insider tells the paper he is "seen as the perfect brainbox nerd with a comic delivery".

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: 'This is for the kiddies' and 'Benefits and pensions chaos'

title: Sandpapergate: Michael Vaughan says Cricket Australia may not like forum findings
description: Cricket Australia (CA) will not like what it finds from a forum into the sandpaper scandal, according to former England captain Michael Vaughan.CA has
body: Cricket Australia (CA) will not like what it finds from a forum into the sandpaper scandal, according to former England captain Michael Vaughan.CA has invited evidence into the ball-tampering controversy of Australia's Test against South Africa in Cape Town in 2018 following weeks of speculation over which players and coaches were involved."It's very clear to me that Cricket Australia are going to find some things out that they're probably not going to want to find out," Vaughan told the Test Match Special podcast."If they don't release the truth of what they find in this forum out to the public, we're going to get back to square one."The row over the ball-tampering scandal was reignited by claims published in the autobiography of former Australia batter Usman Khawaja.At the time of the controversy, only batter Cameron Bancroft, then captain Steve Smith and his deputy David Warner were punished for the cheating plot.Khawaja alleged all players and coaches knew of the tampering and should have taken responsibility, a testimony supported by Bancroft, Warner and squad players Chadd Sayers and Jon Holland.Former coach Darren Lehmann and Australia captain Pat Cummins have been among those who have denied knowledge or involvement.In an attempt to calm the row that has engulfed Australian sport, CA has established a six-week forum for players, coaches and staff involved in 2018 to give evidence to senior counsel Fiona McLeod.Although McLeod will publish her findings and CA will give a public response, evidence will remain confidential, there will be no new attribution of responsibility and no further sanctions.The scope of the forum will extend to the Australian home season prior to the 2018 tour of South Africa, which included their 4-0 Ashes defeat of England.Writing in his autobiography in 2019, former England opener and captain Sir Alastair Cook said the tourists had suspicions about how Australia were getting the ball to move, and that Warner later admitted to using substances attached to the strapping on his hands in domestic matches.Cook's suspicions related to the third Test in Perth. Heavy overnight rain had delayed the fifth day at the Waca, when England were attempting to save the Test.When play finally began, the outfield was wet, conditions that would normally prevent any reverse swing. Cook claimed that Australia found an "inordinate" amount of reverse.Former England batter Dawid Malan was at the crease on the final morning and told BBC Sport: "The amount it did move on a wet day, maybe something was being done to get that ball moving. "That's not me accusing anyone of doing it, but you look and think: 'Yeah, maybe there was something to get the ball moving that much on that last day'."Left-hander Malan scored more runs - 383 - and faced more deliveries - 897 - than any other England batter in that series."You look back and think did the ball start reversing at any times? In some of the games we were probably guilty of not batting long enough for the ball to start reversing."The standout for me would have been that Perth Test, day five. It had rained quite a lot and there was a good little wet patch on the wicket. Batting in that innings, it was quite evident the ball was reversing. I'm not for one minute saying people were scratching the ball or putting anything on it."Whether or not they were tampering with the ball then is not my knowledge, but the ball was swinging a lot more in that series. Maybe, in hindsight, things had started then and they were trying to reverse it."Asked about what the CA forum could uncover about the 2017-18 Ashes, Vaughan said: "From my cricket experience and a cynical look at the past of what may or may not have happened, I don't think Cricket Australia are going to like what they find."Do they make that all public? There's no way in a million years that more people didn't know something was happening to a ball."Despite the potential implications for a series result against England, the England and Wales Cricket Board has not contacted CA about the forum and has no plans to do so.Announcing the forum, CA chair David Boon said: "It is very important to understand that it will not seek to sanction or recriminate."And Vaughan agreed that the governing body should not seek to impose new punishments."You can't go back and punish people," said Vaughan, who famously led England to victory in the 2005 Ashes. "The punishment was far too harsh for the three players at the time. Darren Lehmann lost his job as coach for Australia - there's four people who were really punished."The tampering of a ball is almost the smallest part of the story now. "Some have said that they had no clue sandpaper was used. I understand that, they can have that opinion. The more different aspects of this story that come to light, the more there is that element of do you believe those people? You have to say I'm not too sure about that now."

schema.headline: Sandpapergate: Michael Vaughan says Cricket Australia may not like forum findings

title: A clinic is reassessing people with ADHD and autism diagnoses - but critics fear it could deepen stigma
description: Image source, BBC / WOODY MORRISImage caption, Johanna, 24, began questioning her ADHD diagnosis when she discovered it could act as a barrier to beco
body: Image source, BBC / WOODY MORRISImage caption, Johanna, 24, began questioning her ADHD diagnosis when she discovered it could act as a barrier to becoming a police officerByKate BowieGlobal Health Freya looks nervous as she walks into a psychiatric clinic in Sweden for an ADHD assessment.Countries around the world have seen a huge increase in ADHD diagnoses over recent decades. For many people this can be life changing, helping them understand themselves better and access support.But Freya (not her real name) is not attending a long-awaited appointment to secure a diagnosis.This government-funded clinic offers autism and ADHD diagnosis reassessments - its doctors believe it is the first in the world dedicated solely to this purpose.At 12, Freya was struggling with anxiety at school and sought out professional help. "They thought I had ADHD," she says.But as she grew up, she felt that she did not experience ADHD symptoms. "I don't think I had it in the first place," she now says.Her doubts about the diagnosis became more pressing as a teenager, when she discovered that in Sweden, it could be a barrier to pursuing her dream career of joining the police."I want to have every option open," she tells BBC World Service.If the doctors at the clinic decide Freya does not meet the ADHD criteria, her medical records will be updated, and it will be easier for her to apply for a job with the police.The clinic, known as Mottagning Neuropsykiatri, has opened at a time when rates of ADHD and autism diagnoses are under the spotlight. Many say this is because of greater awareness of the symptoms, and that previously neglected groups - particularly women and girls - are finally getting the diagnoses they need, while others argue that the growing numbers stem from overdiagnosis.The existence of the clinic is controversial. Clinical guidance from UK governing bodies and the World Health Organization describe autism as a lifelong condition and ADHD as a neurodevelopmental condition that can persist into adulthood. The medical consensus is that both diagnoses last a lifetime, even if symptoms fluctuate.And some neurodiversity advocates warn that a dedicated reassessment service could reinforce the idea that being diagnosed with ADHD or autism is undesirable – and deepen the stigma surrounding both conditions.Despite this, hundreds of people have approached the clinic about reassessment.Image source, BBC / WOODY MORRISImage caption, Psychologist Sebastian Lundström runs the clinic, which operates one day a monthBarred from jobsLike Freya, other young adults have been prompted to reconsider their diagnosis after they felt it had become a barrier.This is because historically, Swedes with ADHD or autism were barred from certain jobs, including joining the military, and becoming police officers, train drivers and pilots. This is despite research suggesting some neurodivergent traits can be strengths in certain roles. No such bans exist in the UK, although rules differ globally.Since 2022, people with ADHD have been able to join the Swedish military if they are medication-free. And since 2021, people with ADHD or autism have been able to apply to join the police, but must submit a medical certificate, which can cost around 15,000 SEK (£1,100) privately.When Freya was referred to the clinic, she says she was relieved to find out she could get her diagnosis reassessed there for free.Johanna, 24, was diagnosed with ADHD at 14 after what she describes as a period of bad behaviour at school. She found the diagnosis helpful at first and received additional support from teachers.But as she grew into adulthood, she says she stopped feeling that she needed extra support. And after discovering it was a barrier to becoming a police officer, she began questioning whether it was even accurate.Johanna says she has some traits of ADHD, such as a short attention span, "but not enough to have an ADHD diagnosis," she believes.Johanna was reassessed aged 21 during an early pilot of the reassessment clinic and was found not to meet its diagnostic criteria for ADHD. She now works for her father's company, and does not plan on becoming a police officer.What is an ADHD or autism reassessment?Both ADHD and autism are neurodevelopmental conditions that affect how people think and interact with the world. They are diagnosed through detailed assessments, which can include questionnaires and interviews, rather than one single clinical test.The doctors at Mottagning Neuropsykiatri say their approach is different from traditional assessments, as it focuses less on someone's history, and more on the symptoms they are experiencing in the present."This is not de-diagnosing, this is a renewed assessment of your functioning today," says Sebastian Lundström, the clinic's lead psychologist.The doctors say they do not judge whether the original assessment was correct, so rather than wiping the original diagnosis from patients' medical records, they add a note of the new assessment.Lundström says that some people who once had a diagnosis but are found to not meet the criteria at the clinic may have been misdiagnosed. But he also believes that for a small minority, ADHD and autism are not lifelong conditions and individuals may stop experiencing symptoms as they grow older.But updating a person's diagnosis because they are not currently showing symptoms is a contested approach."We have to remember that these are lifelong conditions," says Navid Ghannad, chair of Autism Skåne, a local Swedish non-profit for autistic people and their families."Because at a certain point in their adulthood during a clinical setting they have had their diagnosis removed, it doesn't necessarily mean that the ADHD or the autism has disappeared," he adds.Symptoms could reappear later in life, he says. "The problem is once they resurface, that individual which doesn't have a diagnosis any longer, they will not be able to get the timely and correct support."Lundström says he does not consider it a big risk that people could get reassessed and find themselves without necessary support.During the pilot he encountered people who "really wanted" to get rid of their diagnosis but the psychologist said, "we still feel that you meet the criteria".Image source, BBC / WOODY MORRISImage caption, Vilda, 22, sought reassessment of her autism diagnosis as she feels she was misdiagnosed 'I was stuck'Vilda, 22, sought reassessment of her autism diagnosis which was initially given after she experienced a trauma."I didn't recognise myself in the description of autism," she says. "I was stuck. I know that this is not me, but I can't do anything about it."It was requests from people like Johanna and Vilda that led to the establishment of the clinic, Lundström explains."It gained momentum by itself and the word spread around. A lot of people contacted us and we felt that there was a justification for starting up," he says. It is only open one day a month.Before opening the clinic, Lundström conducted a small peer-reviewed study - of the 72 individuals who took part, roughly 80% did not meet the criteria for ADHD or autism. All the participants already wanted to lose their diagnosis, rather than being a randomly selected group."It's important to stress that this patient population is not necessarily representative for all with autism and ADHD," he adds.During the first year of the pilot some 400 to 500 people spoke to Lundström, who is also associate professor of child and adolescent psychiatric sciences at the University of Gothenburg, about getting a reassessment.The project also has the backing of senior figures in Swedish psychiatry, including Sophia Eberhard, a senior consultant specialising in child and adolescent psychiatry."It's psychiatry who in the beginning made those diagnoses," she says. "I believe we have a responsibility to help these young adults on their way."In September, the BBC was given permission to join Freya as she became the first patient to attend the newly opened clinic, which serves both men and women.During her appointment, Freya takes part in questionnaires and verbal assessments to see if she meets the ADHD criteria. The process is the same for both ADHD and autism, although the questions differ.Freya says she is hopeful that she will be able to "get rid" of her ADHD diagnosis after the appointment.But the doctors are adamant that they do not just give attendees the outcome they want. They conduct other checks such as assessing body language and communication skills, speaking to younger patients' parents, and checking medical files for ongoing treatment.Image source, BBC / WOODY MORRISImage caption, Navid Ghannad, chair of Autism Skåne, a local Swedish non-profit for autistic people, says it is important to remember autism and ADHD are lifelong conditionsFears about stigmaThe opening of the clinic has drawn criticism from those who fear it sends the wrong message about autism and ADHD."The clinic presents neurodiversity and autistic people as a bad thing, like we are a problem that needs to be fixed - we are not," says Jenny Hedin, from charity Organiserade Autister Västernorrland, an advocacy organisation run by and for autistic adults.Hedin, who is autistic and has ADHD, warns that people who can successfully "mask" or mimic neurotypical behaviour might feel under pressure to lose their diagnosis in order to be better accepted by society."That is especially a problem with women and girls, because girls are usually great at masking," she adds.Others say the focus should be on changing the rules that make it difficult for people with ADHD or autism to pursue certain careers.Eric Donell, the chairman of Riksförbundet Attention, a national Swedish charity, lobbies to remove employment restrictions affecting neurodivergent people, which he says are unfair.He stresses that for many people, getting a diagnosis is extremely important. "Instead of asking people to get rid of their diagnosis, sometimes we should just ask whether the rules themselves are justified," he says.Reassessments risk becoming "a way of adapting the individual to society instead of adapting society to human differences," he adds.'Magic spell'People from the UK, Denmark, Norway and Germany have also been in touch for reassessment, says Lundström, but they have been turned away, as the clinic only serves locals.Georgina, 35, from the UK, contacted the clinic because she wants to have the autism diagnosis she received at 25 "removed"."It felt like a magic spell, that I'd get this label and the world would be more understanding," she says.Instead, she says, her colleagues belittled her.Georgina has since been offered an NHS reassessment. The process is the same as the original assessment she went through, and can result in patients receiving more diagnoses, fewer diagnoses or no change.The Swedish reassessment clinic says they generally would not apply new or additional diagnoses to people - something Georgina was attracted to."The situation where you can go in and then come out with other labels... that's really off-putting," she says. For now, she has decided not to undergo an NHS reassessment. Instead, she is trying to find out how often a diagnosis is reconsidered, before deciding whether to go ahead.Back in Sweden, a few hours after Freya entered the clinic, she re-emerges from a consultation room. The doctors here have found that, right now, she does not meet the criteria for an ADHD diagnosis.She says it is "confirmation" that she was right to question her diagnosis."Now, finally, I have the same opportunity as everyone else."

schema.headline: A clinic is reassessing people with ADHD and autism diagnoses - but critics fear it could deepen stigma

title: Charity set up in Captain Sir Tom Moore's name bids to be struck off
description: A charity set up by the family of renowned pandemic fundraiser Capt Sir Tom Moore has applied to be struck off.The charity is now known as the 1189808
body: A charity set up by the family of renowned pandemic fundraiser Capt Sir Tom Moore has applied to be struck off.The charity is now known as the 1189808 Foundation, having dropped Sir Tom's name at the request of his family last year.An application to have it struck off appeared on the Companies House register on Friday.The World War Two veteran became a household name during the first Covid-19 lockdown, raising £39.4m for NHS charities by walking laps of the garden at his home in Marston Moretaine, Bedfordshire.However, the charity founded in his name became mired in controversy after the charities watchdog found misconduct and mismanagement on the part of his daughter and her husband in their running of it.The Charity Commission's report uncovered a "repeated pattern of behaviour" through which Hannah Ingram-Moore and her husband, Colin, made private gains and which the regulator said would have left people feeling "misled".A £1.4m book deal and an £18,000 awards ceremony appearance fee were among the financial benefits the Ingram-Moores were found to have enjoyed through the Captain Tom Foundation.They have already been banned from being charity trustees and earlier resigned from the foundation.The millions raised by the late Sir Tom and donated to NHS Charities Together before the foundation was formed were not part of the commission's inquiry.The father-of-two died aged 100 in February 2021 with coronavirus.Do you have a story suggestion for Beds, Herts or Bucks? Contact us below.

title: Chicken Shop Date: The perfect end or a disappointing send-off?
description: Image source, Dimz IncImage caption, After more than 10 years, Amelia Dimoldenberg announced Chicken Shop Date was shutting up shopByRiyah CollinsBBC
body: Image source, Dimz IncImage caption, After more than 10 years, Amelia Dimoldenberg announced Chicken Shop Date was shutting up shopByRiyah CollinsBBC NewsbeatFor better or worse, everyone recalls their first date. But how will the last one be remembered?After more than a decade of serving up her awkward, off-the-wall questions, Amelia Dimoldenberg's Chicken Shop Date is no longer looking for love, with the YouTuber calling time on her hit series.From a youth club project to a full-blown media empire with A-listers asking her out, the series has influenced the interview landscape and carved a new path for the next generation of content creators. "To start my next chapter, I have to close this one," Dimoldenberg told the BBC earlier this month. "I'm focussing on making sure I say goodbye in the perfect way so I feel ready to do my next thing."This article contains spoilers for the final episode of Chicken Shop Date. After much speculation as to who would be the final date, fans were never going to be able to agree as to whether the farewell was indeed perfect.Names like Harry Styles and Beyoncé had been floated around, but it was Drake who was the favourite with some bookies after Dimoldenberg previously described the Canadian rapper as her dream date.So when the camera panned to psychotherapist Esther Perel, "everyone was a bit surprised", says fan Sarah Almond, who watched an early cinema screening on Tuesday.Image source, Dimz IncImage caption, Relationships expert Perel is also a bestselling author and podcast host"I wasn't familiar with Esther Perel myself and I don't think anyone else in the cinema was aware of who she was," the content creator tells BBC Newsbeat.And when the episode went live on YouTube, while most viewers reacted positively to the choice of guest, some said they did not recognise her and asked "where's Drake?!"."I did hear a few people say they were disappointed, but I wasn't disappointed at all," Almond says."Even though I was expecting a bigger name to go off with a big bang, it was exactly what the show needed."The episode played out like a counselling session, becoming emotional at points, Almond says."She's treating the end of Chicken Shop Date like it's a relationship break-up."It served her really well. It was a nice goodbye."Image source, Sarah AlmondImage caption, Sarah Almond says the final episode was "bittersweet" but a fitting end for the series Signing off with an interview with a relationships expert is a sign of the journey Dimoldenberg has been on with her pioneering series. With more than three million YouTube subscribers, Chicken Shop Date has climbed the pecking order to become a key stop on press tours for even some of the world's biggest names, including the likes of Cher and Sir Paul McCartney.But it wasn't always that way.Rachel Adeolu watched the series from the very beginning, when Dimoldenberg would mostly date emerging rap and grime artists."A chicken shop is somewhere that's very familiar to a lot of people who grew up in London," the 21-year-old says. "It's kind of like a third space where a lot of us built friendships."So seeing content creators who also looked like us being interviewed in that same kind of setting with this unconventional interview style, which was also very funny, was unheard of."Image source, Rachel AdeoluImage caption, Rachel Adeolu was a fan of how the series represented black culture when it first started By 2021, seven years on from the first episode, the show was starting to look different. As well as rappers and content creators, Dimoldenberg was bagging interviews with pop stars like Ed Sheeran and Finneas, as well as footballers Tammy Abraham and John Stones.It was about that time producer Liv West joined the team, and her background at a major music publisher helped the series secure an impressive roster of guests."That summer we had a really big line-up," she says, with the likes of Keke Palmer, Charli XCX and Rosalía looking for love at first bite."It was then we started to think the tides are changing," she adds.Image source, Liv WestImage caption, Liv West was a producer on Chicken Shop Date for almost five years As the profiles of the dates grew though, so did their teams, with West saying it became a challenge to squeeze everyone in for shoots - with some being put into the kitchen.The producer feels things ramped up after the episode with documentary maker Louis Theroux, as he was not a typical guest and of "legendary status".For earlier fans like Adeolu, the take-off came at a cost."It feels like the audience who are more interested in seeing A-list celebrities be interviewed, they have definitely been favoured over the people who made the show popular in the first place," she says."In terms of just the initial charm of what the show was, I think that has probably had a negative impact on it."Image source, Dimz IncImage caption, Dimoldenberg has collaborated with Theroux multiple times since their date in 2022As Dimoldenberg reached new audiences, her success started to balloon and before long she was appearing on major red carpets, in films and magazines - as well as a guest on other people's talk shows.It also allowed her to work on a passion project: Dimz Inc Academy. Launched in 2025, the scheme aims to upskill and mentor young people from underrepresented backgrounds who want to get into creative industries."It was Amelia's big dream to really make the creative industry, and particularly digital entertainment, accessible from every walk of life for every young person," West says.Now in its second year, the scheme will be a legacy for the series away from screens - but as for what's next for the series' star, that's yet to be revealed."I really want to spend more time writing, that's what I'd like to focus on in the future," Dimoldenberg told the BBC."But who knows, the possibilities are endless."Additional reporting by Naomi Clarke, Miya Chahal and Srosh Khan. Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here.

schema.headline: Chicken Shop Date: The perfect end or a disappointing send-off?
